title: The Choir of Vessel Farm
premise: Lena Underhill takes a teaching post at Vessel Farm Primary, a rural school where children vanish from the registers one by one and the staff's nightly sleep recordings capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud. As Lena investigates, she learns the school was built over an old congregational singing hall where a choir drowned mid-hymn, and that the missing children have been recruited to finish the song the dead began. The voice offers her power—her brother back from the coma he's lain in for three years—in exchange for joining the choir. In the end, Lena refuses the bargain, teaches the children the song's final verse as a counter-song of their own names spoken aloud, breaking the choir's hold at the cost of her brother waking without any memory of her.
about_author: Isandro Joubert is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in farming communities across the interior before turning to writing full-time. Their fiction draws on folk hymnody, classroom folklore, and the particular loneliness of small-town institutions.

chapters.title: The Register
chapters.summary: Lena arrives at Vessel Farm Primary and notices twenty-six names on the class list but only nineteen desks occupied. The headmaster, Mr. Calloway, waves away her questions with practiced ease. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: wary curiosity masking the grief she's carrying about her comatose brother, Daniel.

chapters.title: Nineteen Desks
chapters.summary: Lena settles into teaching and befriends quiet student Wren Halloway, who draws the same spiral shape in every notebook margin. A colleague, Mrs. Okafor, warns her not to learn the children's middle names. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: growing attachment to the students, first prickle of unease.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: A boy named Tomas fails to arrive; his desk is removed overnight and his name struck from the register before anyone reports him missing. Calloway claims the family moved. Lena finds Tomas's half-finished workbook in the incinerator ash. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: disbelief hardening into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Sleep Study
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okafor reveals the staff participate in a district-mandated sleep recording program, ostensibly for wellness research. She plays Lena a tape: her own sleeping breath, then a second voice—dry, choral, many-throated—answering questions in the pauses. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: cold dread; the rational scaffolding begins to crack.

chapters.title: What the Tape Answers
chapters.summary: Lena experiments, speaking questions aloud before bed. The morning recording contains answers: precise, intimate, including details about Daniel's hospital room. She confronts Calloway, who goes pale and begs her to stop asking. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: terror braided with temptation—the voice knows things it shouldn't.

chapters.title: Wren's Verse
chapters.summary: Wren hums a melody no one taught her; three other children join in harmony they couldn't know. When Lena asks where they learned it, Wren says, 'From under the floor.' The school sits atop the ruins of the old Vessel congregational hall. POV: alternating Lena and Wren. Emotional beat: innocence turned uncanny.

chapters.title: The Drowned Choir
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Lena finds the 1911 record: forty-one singers drowned when the hall flooded during a midnight rehearsal, mid-verse. The hymn was never finished; local belief holds an unfinished song keeps its singers. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: grim comprehension—the missing children are being conscripted.

chapters.title: Okafor's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Okafor admits the sleep program isn't district-run; the staff record themselves to monitor who the voice has 'marked.' Her own sister vanished decades ago. She shows Lena the tapes of every teacher since 1962—all ending the same way. POV: Okafor. Emotional beat: weary guilt, a plea for alliance.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The voice speaks to Lena directly through the recorder: it can return Daniel, whole and walking, if she lends it her voice to complete the verse. It demonstrates—a nurse calls the hospital; Daniel's fingers moved yesterday. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: love against duty; the bargain glitters.

chapters.title: Twenty-Four
chapters.summary: Another child, Priya, is gone; nineteen desks become eighteen. Lena finds the register rewritten in ink that is still wet. Calloway confesses he gave his own son to the choir years ago to save the rest, and believes sacrifice is arithmetic. POV: Calloway. Emotional beat: corrupted duty; power rationalizing atrocity.

chapters.title: Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Lena breaks into the sealed cellar and finds the flooded hall preserved below: pews, a raised conductor's dais, and forty-one outlines worn into the stone where the choir stood. The water is still there, black and patient, though no flood could reach this depth. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: visceral horror; the scale of the thing.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: At night the school hums. Through the classroom floorboards Lena watches the missing children standing in the flooded hall, singing beneath the water without drowning, learning the verse line by line. Wren looks up at her through the dark water and mouths: help us. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: heartbreak; they are still children.

chapters.title: Daniel Wakes
chapters.summary: The voice makes good partially: Daniel opens his eyes, responsive but vacant, waiting. The doctors call it a miracle. Lena understands it's a down payment—and that the balance comes due when the song finishes. POV: Lena, intercut with a phone call home. Emotional beat: joy curdling into debt.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Sacrifice
chapters.summary: Calloway moves to formalize the next offering, arguing one child now saves nineteen later. Okafor sides with him out of exhaustion. Lena realizes the staff were never wardens—they were recruiters who lost their nerve. POV: Calloway. Emotional beat: power's self-justifying logic laid bare.

chapters.title: Wren Runs
chapters.summary: Wren flees the school rather than be taken; the choir's pull drags her sleepwalking back toward the farm each night. Lena barricades them both in her cottage and discovers salt and spoken names slow the pull—but only while Wren hears her own name said with love. POV: alternating Lena and Wren. Emotional beat: fierce protectiveness; a clue disguised as tenderness.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Okafor translates the hymnal fragment: the final verse was never written down because the composer intended it to be improvised—each singer naming themselves into the song. The choir cannot finish it alone; it needs living voices who choose to sing. That's why it recruits instead of taking by force. POV: Okafor. Emotional beat: revelation; the trap has a seam.

chapters.title: Calloway's Bargain
chapters.summary: Calloway offers himself to the choir in exchange for leaving the children, but the voice rejects him—he has no song left, only obedience. His collapse reveals the truth: the voice doesn't want the willing old, it wants the unspent young. POV: Calloway. Emotional beat: the corrupter discarded by what he served.

chapters.title: Choosing to Sing
chapters.summary: Lena resolves to enter the hall and teach the children the counter-song: their own names, their own verses, sung against the hymn. Okafor gives her the original tuning fork from the 1911 hall. Daniel's vacancy deepens—the voice tightening its hold as leverage. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: resolve; love choosing duty freely.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Lena wades into the black water of the drowned hall, the choir rising around her in forty-one shapes. They offer Daniel again, fully restored, if she'll simply take the melody and carry it up. She begins to hum—and feels her own name start to dissolve. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: climax threshold; the price made flesh.

chapters.title: The Counter-Song
chapters.summary: Instead of the hymn, Lena sings the children's names—Wren first, then all the taken—and the children's voices break from the choir's harmony to answer with verses of their own making. The unfinished song, given its true last verse, ends. The water drains; the shapes come apart like breath on glass. POV: Lena and Wren together. Emotional beat: catharsis; love sung louder than power.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The children wake in the cornfield above the collapsed cellar, alive and ordinary. The school closes; Okafor burns the tapes; Calloway is found sitting in an empty classroom, unable to say what he lost. The voice is gone—or waiting somewhere new. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: exhausted relief shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Lena visits Daniel, awake and healthy and looking at her with polite blankness—the price of survival paid in full. She tells him stories about a brother she says she once knew, and Wren, holding her hand, quietly says Lena's name aloud, just to hear it answered. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; what remains when the song is done.
